title: Hypertrophy Q&A #5
summary: Monthly Q&A covering squat and deadlift scheduling, building a back without rows, rep range matching, close grip bench versus skull crushers, pull-up progression, minimal-equipment training, supersets and session length, his workout log, six-day splits, men versus women hypertrophy, jawline training and pre-fatigue.
claims: Never do heavy squats and heavy deadlifts on the same day or on back-to-back days; they are the most draining lifts and must be spaced out
In a 4-day split: upper day 1, lower day 2 opened by heavy squat, another upper, then lower day 4 opened by heavy deadlift
On a lower day you can still do lighter hinge or squat variations with less taxing styles and higher reps, focused on volume and form
RDLs do not represent the deadlift on an intensity day; you need a heavy deadlift style that emphasizes the concentric
He does not separate volume and intensity days; lower-intensity work comes as back-off sets or higher-rep variations, which do not replace strength work
The deep ab 'cut' is the ridge between the muscle walls; reveal it by staying relatively lean and growing the abs so they bulge
He trains abs every day because they recover fast; the core must be trained directly, not treated as a by-product
You can build a big back with only deadlifts and weighted pull-ups: deadlift is king, then vertical pull, with horizontal rows the lame duck of the family
Back thickness comes from the deadlift, not necessarily rows
A shrug done hip-hinged forward is a vertical pull that hits the mid back
Barbell rows tax the lower back like a deadlift without leg drive; dumbbell or seal rows avoid the hip hinge if your back suffers
Matching rep ranges between overhead press and bench is bro science; you are much stronger horizontally anyway
If overhead press opens the day as strength work, 12-15 reps is too many; use about 3-6 reps; 8-10 on bench is fine

Close grip bench and skull crushers are not interchangeable: close grip is a horizontal press hitting lateral and medial triceps heads plus chest and shoulders, skull crushers with shoulder flexion target the long head
Skull crushers do almost nothing for the bench; close grip bench carries over to it
If you add close grip bench, put it on a non-bench day, e.g. bench on Monday and close grip late in the week
Negative pull-ups can go first in the workout before squats or deadlifts since they take nothing from those lifts; use straps if grip is an issue
Splitting training into two daily sessions is valid, as Olympic lifters do; use one session for volume and one for intensity and hit different muscles
He started with knee push-ups and pink dumbbells, did dumbbell-only workouts daily for about three years, then five years of barbell training
People with small arms just do not train them; train them for years and they grow
To progress pull-ups use grease the groove, higher frequency or overload; mixed grips make them non-taxing, so you can push volume hard
Overreach pull-ups for a week, rest 2-3 days, and you will likely hit a PR; he does pull-ups every day
With only a pull-up bar, dip bars and 2 kg kettlebells: tons of kettlebell swings like cardio, uphill lunges, kettlebell RDLs, goblet squats, knee raises and band arm work
Upper A/B/C rotations may be too much; spreading C into A and B keeps specificity and relevant tonnage
Rotating similar lifts lowers overuse injury risk by changing joint angles but reduces practice on each lift
A lift that is intensity-focused on day A stays intensity-focused on day B; do not rotate volume and intensity on top of exercises
If the same work fits in one hour with supersets as in two hours, the two-hour session was lazy with excess rest; if not, you were under-resting or digging too deep into the baseline
Properly done supersets do not hurt performance much; the tradeoff with tonnage accumulation is in your favor
He logs evolving rep ranges in shorthand: 5 means 5-4, 6 means 6-5-4, 7 means 7-5-3, 8 means 8-6-4, then resets with more weight
He keeps a separate workout plan and log; each day has six main exercises in supersets that rotate in and out after the strength work, which always happens
Six days a week suits novices who recover fast, or advanced lifters needing frequency to accumulate volume
If six days feels wrong, fit the same volume into four days and use the two rest days to recover
He does not recommend deloads: the need can be prevented inside the program and bodybuilding has no peak
For injuries use high-rep strength restoration outside relevant intensity windows to grease the movement and send blood, not heavy high-rep sets
He used the one-arm cable row only as a pump finisher on deadlift days for the horizontal stretch; pull-ups and rows build lats better
Machine strength varies little whether done at the start or end of a workout, unlike free weights
Men are built to be more muscular: larger upper body, denser bones and muscles, different attachments; androgen receptors are useless without androgens
Upper body development bias is both biology and culture: women train arms less and see less impressive results
Be careful greasing the groove on multi-joint barbell lifts due to overuse injury; beginners should just lift heavy and go home
Front levers are not comparable to pullovers: the lats stabilize rather than move, without the stretch
Jaw muscles can grow but jawline is largely genetic; jaw training stresses the teeth and risks painful tension, not worth it
Real pre-fatigue with heavy flyes before bench is bad, but a light band fly for pump does not attack the baseline and helps activate the chest
exercises: lats stabilize, not a pullover substitute
